column1: What duration defines an acute fever during pediatric clinical evaluation?
column2: Acute fever is defined as a fever lasting less than 7 days.

column1: How is the Hess test (tourniquet test) performed for suspected Dengue?
column2: A blood pressure cuff is inflated on the forearm to midway between systolic and diastolic pressure ($\frac{\text{SBP} + \text{DBP}}{2}$) for 5 minutes.

column1: What count of petechiae per square inch defines a positive Hess test result?
column2: Greater than 20 petechiae per square inch (with $\ge 10$ also considered positive in revised guidelines).

column1: Which diagnostic test has the highest positive yield during the first two days of Dengue fever?
column2: Dengue NS1 Antigen (NS1 Ag) test.

column1: What are three key warning signs indicating Dengue with warning signs (Group B2)?
column2: Persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, and mucosal bleeding (or lethargy/restlessness and fluid accumulation).

column1: What primary laboratory parameters must be monitored in suspected Dengue fever?
column2: Complete Blood Count (WBC, Platelets) and Hematocrit / Packed Cell Volume (PCV).

column1: What fluid choice is indicated during the critical phase of Dengue for children over 6 months of age?
column2: Isotonic intravenous fluids (such as 0.9% Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate).

column1: What fluid modification is considered for infants under 6 months old during the critical phase of Dengue?
column2: Half-strength saline should be considered.

column1: What fever-related criterion must be satisfied prior to discharging a recovered Dengue patient?
column2: Absence of fever for at least 48 hours without the use of antipyretic medications.

column1: Why is the day of defervescence (fever reduction) critical in Dengue clinical management?
column2: It marks the start of the critical phase, where systemic plasma leakage and shock are most likely to develop.

column1: Why are Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) like Ibuprofen contraindicated in Dengue?
column2: They aggravate platelet dysfunction and significantly increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.

column1: Which antipyretic is safe for fever management in suspected Dengue infection?
column2: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen).

column1: What narrow pulse pressure value indicates impending or active Dengue shock?
column2: A pulse pressure less than or equal to 20 mmHg ($\le 20\ \text{mmHg}$).

column1: What class of pathogens causes most cases of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in children under 5 years old?
column2: Viruses (most commonly Respiratory Syncytial Virus / RSV).

column1: According to BTS guidelines, are routine microbiological investigations recommended for mild pediatric CAP treated in the community?
column2: No, microbiological testing is not routinely recommended for mild CAP or outpatient management.

column1: In which pediatric CAP cases are microbiological investigations indicated?
column2: In severe pneumonia requiring intensive care or in cases with persistent complications.

column1: Is a routine follow-up chest X-ray required for a previously healthy child recovering well from CAP?
column2: No, follow-up radiography is not required in children who were previously healthy and are recovering well.

column1: What clinical or radiological features mandate a follow-up chest radiograph after pediatric CAP?
column2: Round pneumonia, lobar collapse, or persisting respiratory symptoms.

column1: What is Primary Tuberculosis in pediatric patients?
column2: TB infection occurring upon the initial exposure of a pathogen-naive individual to *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*.

column1: What defines Secondary or Reactivation Tuberculosis?
column2: TB disease occurring in a person who was previously infected with *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*.

column1: How many effective drugs should be included in an initial pediatric tuberculosis treatment regimen?
column2: At least 4 drugs to which the organism is sensitive or the patient is treatment-naive.

column1: What drug delivery strategy is mandatory for pediatric tuberculosis therapy adherence?
column2: Daily Directly Observed Therapy (DOT).

column1: What is the minimum treatment duration for minimal pediatric pulmonary TB after achieving a negative culture?
column2: At least 12 months after the last negative culture.

column1: What is the recommended treatment duration for extensive pediatric pulmonary tuberculosis with cavitary disease?
column2: At least 18 months.

column1: What rule governs regimen modification when managing a failing anti-tuberculosis treatment?
column2: Do not add a single new drug to a failing regimen.

column1: Why is source case tracing vital when evaluating a child with tuberculosis?
column2: Children contract TB from infected adult contacts; identifying the adult source confirms sensitivity patterns and prevents further transmission.

column1: What functional airway abnormality represents the primary pathophysiological feature of asthma?
column2: Bronchial hyperresponsiveness (airway hyperreactivity) coupled with chronic inflammation and variable airflow obstruction.

column1: What diagnostic trial is recommended for suspected asthma in children under 5 years old?
column2: An 8-week trial of a pediatric moderate dose of Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS).

column1: What step should be taken following an 8-week trial of ICS in a child under 5 if symptoms persist?
column2: Stop the ICS treatment and re-evaluate for an alternative diagnosis.

column1: What presentation warrants an 8-week trial of moderate-dose ICS in a child under 5?
column2: Asthma symptoms occurring 3 or more times per week, waking at night, or symptoms uncontrolled on SABA alone.

column1: What is the first-line reliever medication for acute asthma symptoms in children?
column2: Inhaled Short-Acting Beta-Agonist (SABA), such as Salbutamol.

column1: What step is recommended for a child aged 5–16 with uncontrolled asthma on low-dose ICS and LABA?
column2: Change maintenance therapy to a MART (Maintenance and Reliever Therapy) regimen with a low maintenance ICS dose.

column1: What does the clinical acronym MART stand for in asthma management?
column2: Maintenance and Reliever Therapy (using a single combination inhaler for daily control and acute relief).

column1: How should therapy be escalated if a child aged 5–16 is uncontrolled on a low-dose ICS MART regimen?
column2: Increase the ICS to a pediatric moderate maintenance dose (continuing MART or switching to fixed-dose ICS/LABA with SABA).

column1: What management action is indicated if suspected asthma in a child under 5 is uncontrolled on low-dose ICS plus an LTRA?
column2: Stop the LTRA and refer the child to a specialist with expertise in pediatric asthma.

column1: What two initial interventions are essential for managing an acute severe asthma exacerbation in a child?
column2: High-flow oxygen and inhaled Short-Acting Beta-Agonist (SABA / Salbutamol).

column1: What target oxygen saturation level should be maintained during acute asthma management in children?
column2: Greater than 92% ($>92\%$).

column1: What physical examination finding on chest auscultation indicates an acute asthma exacerbation?
column2: Bilateral widespread rhonchi (wheezing) without focal crackles.

column1: Why is a spacer device recommended over a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) alone in young children?
column2: It optimizes drug delivery to lower airways and reduces reliance on breathing-coordination technique.

column1: What is the clinical definition of anaphylaxis?
column2: A severe, rapid-onset, potentially life-threatening systemic allergic reaction involving airway, breathing, or circulation.

column1: What is the first-line drug of choice for acute anaphylaxis treatment?
column2: Intramuscular (IM) Epinephrine / Adrenaline ($1:1,000$ concentration).

column1: What is the recommended IM Epinephrine ($1:1,000$) dose for an infant under 6 months old?
column2: $0.1\ \text{mL}$ to $0.15\ \text{mL}$ ($100\ \mu\text{g}$ to $150\ \mu\text{g}$).

column1: What is the recommended IM Epinephrine ($1:1,000$) dose for a child aged 6 months to 6 years?
What is the recommended IM Epinephrine ($1:1,000$) dose for a child aged 6 to 12 years?
What is the recommended IM Epinephrine ($1:1,000$) dose for adolescents over 12 years and adults?
What is the preferred injection site for IM epinephrine in pediatric anaphylaxis?
column2: The anterolateral aspect of the middle third of the thigh (vastus lateralis muscle).

column1: At what frequency can IM epinephrine be repeated if anaphylactic symptoms persist?
column2: Every 5 minutes.

column1: How is refractory anaphylaxis defined?
column2: Persistence of anaphylactic shock or respiratory distress despite administration of 2 proper doses of IM adrenaline.

column1: What single factor represents the greatest risk for fatal anaphylaxis and biphasic reactions?
column2: Delayed administration of epinephrine.

column1: What is the primary pharmacological treatment step for refractory anaphylaxis?
column2: Intravenous (IV) low-dose epinephrine infusion.

column1: Should IM adrenaline injections be paused while preparing an IV adrenaline infusion for refractory anaphylaxis?
column2: No, IM adrenaline injections should continue every 5 minutes until the IV adrenaline infusion is actively running.

column1: What level-of-care setting is required for managing refractory anaphylaxis?
column2: Intensive Care Unit (ICU) setting with continuous monitoring and advanced life support.

column1: What fluid intervention is essential during refractory anaphylactic shock?
column2: Rapid IV crystalloid fluid boluses via large-bore IV access to expand intravascular volume.

column1: What classic symptom triad characterizes Acute Epiglottitis?
column2: High fever, severe respiratory distress with stridor, and drooling of saliva.

column1: What posture is typically assumed by a child with acute epiglottitis?
column2: Sitting upright and leaning forward with head extended ("tripod" position).

column1: What organism is the most common cause of Acute Epiglottitis in unimmunized children?
column2: *Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib).

column1: Why is direct throat visualization strictly avoided in suspected acute epiglottitis?
column2: Physical examination of the pharynx can trigger lethal laryngospasm and total airway occlusion.

column1: What definitive airway procedure is indicated for severe acute epiglottitis?
column2: Prophylactic endotracheal intubation in a controlled operating room or ICU environment.

column1: How does Croup (Acute Laryngotracheobronchitis) clinical presentation differ from epiglottitis?
column2: Croup features a characteristic barking cough, hoarseness, low-grade fever, and absence of drooling.

column1: What is the primary medical treatment for moderate-to-severe Croup?
column2: Dexamethasone (oral or IM) and nebulized adrenaline.

column1: What clinical picture suggests Foreign Body Aspiration in a playing toddler?
column2: Sudden onset of choking and paroxysmal coughing with focal wheeze or stridor in an afebrile child.

column1: What pharyngeal feature distinguishes Laryngeal Diphtheria from standard croup?
column2: A adherent greyish pseudomembrane over the larynx/pharynx accompanied by cervical lymphadenopathy ("bull neck").

column1: What specific antitoxin therapy must be administered urgently in cases of Laryngeal Diphtheria?
column2: Intravenous Anti-Diphtheria Toxin (Diphtheria Antitoxin).

column1: How is Failure to Thrive (FTT) defined on a pediatric growth curve?
column2: Weight deceleration crossing 2 or more major centiles or weight remaining consistently below the 3rd percentile.

column1: Are the majority of Failure to Thrive (FTT) cases caused by underlying organic pathology?
column2: No, over 80% ($>80\%$) of cases are non-organic, stemming from environmental, psychosocial, or feeding behavioral factors.

column1: What physical examination finding is most sensitive for acute Testicular Torsion?
column2: Absence of the ipsilateral cremasteric reflex.

column1: What is the critical surgical window to maintain high testicular viability during testicular torsion?
column2: Within 6 hours of symptom onset (salvage rate $>90\%$).

column1: Why must contralateral orchidopexy be performed during surgical correction of unilateral testicular torsion?
column2: The predisposing anatomical anomaly ("bell-clapper" deformity) is bilateral, putting the unaffected testis at risk.

column1: What clinical features differentiate continuous fever from intermittent fever?
column2: Continuous fever remains elevated with minor fluctuations, whereas intermittent fever fluctuates to normal body temperature periodically.

column1: What physical signs indicate plasma leakage in a patient with severe Dengue?
column2: Ascites, pleural effusion, and progressive hemoconcentration (rising PCV).

column1: How does leukopenia and thrombocytopenia assist in diagnosing acute Dengue fever?
column2: Rapidly dropping leukocyte and platelet counts typically accompany the onset of plasma leakage near fever defervescence.

column1: What dosage titration range is used for intravenous epinephrine infusion in refractory anaphylactic shock?
column2: $0.1\ \mu\text{g/kg/min}$ to $1.0\ \mu\text{g/kg/min}$, titrated to systemic perfusion and blood pressure.

column1: What is the role of Leukotriene Receptor Antagonists (LTRAs) in chronic asthma management for children under 5?
column2: Used as an add-on controller option alongside low-dose ICS before specialist referral.

column1: What clinical features signal severe airway edema during acute anaphylaxis?
column2: Inspiratory stridor, voice hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, and progressive upper airway obstruction.

column1: Why is diagnostic Doppler ultrasound contraindicated if clinical suspicion for testicular torsion is high?
column2: Imaging delays definitive surgical exploration and increases the risk of irreversible ischemic testicular necrosis.
